analysis.evidence: יֻלַּד בֵּן means “a son was born.” The prefixed לְ־ identifies Seth, introduced in the preceding verse, as the father. He names the child Enosh.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ־ “and” + preposition לְ־ “to” + masculine singular proper noun שֵׁת.
analysis.sense: the son of Adam and his wife born after Abel’s death

analysis.evidence: In וּלְשֵׁת גַּם הוּא יֻלַּד בֵּן, הוּא refers back to Seth. גַּם marks him as another father in the narrative: “To Seth, too, a son was born.”
analysis.morphology: Invariable additive particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: הוּא refers back to Seth in וּלְשֵׁת. גַּם focuses the pronoun, giving the sense “to Seth, to him too, a son was born.” The לְ on Seth supplies the English “to,” and בֵּן is the subject of the passive verb יֻלַּד.
analysis.morphology: Independent personal pronoun, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: בֵּן (“a son”) is the subject of the passive verb יֻלַּד, and וּלְשֵׁת identifies Seth as the parent to whom the son was born.
analysis.morphology: Pual perfect, third person masculine singular

analysis.evidence: בֵּן is the subject of יֻלַּד “was born.” A son was born to Seth (וּלְשֵׁת), and Seth named him Enosh (אֱנוֹשׁ).
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ אֱנוֹשׁ, אֶת marks שְׁמוֹ (“his name”) as the direct object, and אֱנוֹשׁ supplies the name Seth gave his son.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ and no suffix

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ אֱנוֹשׁ, “he called his name Enosh,” אֶת marks שְׁמוֹ (“his name”) as the direct object of וַיִּקְרָא. The possessive suffix makes שְׁמוֹ definite, and אֱנוֹשׁ supplies the name given.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle, unsuffixed and without a prefix.

analysis.evidence: After reporting the birth of a son to Seth, the verse says וַיִּקְרָא אֶת־שְׁמוֹ אֱנוֹשׁ, “he called his name Enosh.” The naming formula identifies אֱנוֹשׁ as the child’s personal name.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: After Seth names his son Enosh, אָז introduces הוּחַל לִקְרֹא בְּשֵׁם יַהְוֶה, placing the beginning of calling on the name of YHWH at the time just described.
analysis.morphology: Temporal adverb, uninflected, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אָז means “then,” and the following infinitive לִקְרֹא specifies what began. The clause אָז הוּחַל לִקְרֹא בְּשֵׁם יַהְוֶה means “then people began to call on the name of Yahweh.” The Hebrew leaves the callers unnamed.
analysis.morphology: Hophal perfect, third person masculine singular, used impersonally.

analysis.evidence: לִקְרֹא בְּשֵׁם יַהְוֶה means “to call upon the name of YHWH.” The earlier וַיִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ אֱנוֹשׁ gives the child a name. Here בְּשֵׁם introduces the divine name used in invocation.
analysis.morphology: Qal infinitive construct with prefixed לִ־, complementing הוּחַל.

analysis.evidence: In לִקְרֹא בְּשֵׁם יַהְוֶה, “to call on the name of Yahweh,” יַהְוֶה identifies the deity whose name is invoked.
analysis.morphology: Singular proper noun without prefix or suffix
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel
